1.note: Moses is using the adjectives **righteous** and **wicked** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who are righteous … those who are wicked]

2.note: See how you translated “the wicked” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [the wicked person]

Moses is using **a son of striking** as a common expression of his culture to mean that a person deserves to be beaten. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [someone who deserves to be beaten] or [someone who should be beaten]

The expression **be beaten** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone should beat him]

Here, **to his face** represents being in front of the judge who is watching. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of him] or [while he watches]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the wicked things he has done]

3.q: פֶּן־יֹסִ֨יף לְ⁠הַכֹּת֤⁠וֹ עַל־אֵ֨לֶּה֙ מַכָּ֣ה רַבָּ֔ה וְ⁠נִקְלָ֥ה אָחִ֖י⁠ךָ לְ⁠עֵינֶֽי⁠ךָ
3.note: Moses is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the judge an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [in order to prevent him from giving any more blows than these and humiliating your brother before your eyes]

Moses is using the term **brother** to describe someone who is descended from the same ancestor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your fellow Israelite] or [this person]

The expression **is humiliated** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and he becomes ashamed] or [and he feels deep shame]
See how you translated the phrase “before your eyes” in 1:30. Alternate translation: [in your sight]

4.note: A **muzzle** is a device put over an animal’s mouth to prevent it from eating, and **threshing** is the process of separating grain from its stalks by having an animal walk on it or pull a heavy object over it. If your readers would not be familiar with these practices, you could use more general terms or explain them in a footnote. Alternate translation: [You shall not put a covering over an ox’s mouth while it is separating grain] or [You shall not prevent an ox from eating while it is trampling the grain]

5.note: Moses is giving instructions for what should happen to the widow in the possible situation in which **brothers live together and one of them dies, and he does not have a son**. Use a connector that makes it clear that this is what to do if that situation happens. Alternate translation: [then the wife of the dead man shall not marry a strange man from outside]

Moses is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **go in to her**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [have sexual relations with her] or [marry her and consummate the marriage]
Your language may have its own term or expression for the relationship described in **brother-in-law**. Alternate translation: [The brother of her dead husband]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her]

6.note: If your language would not represent this number in a form such as **the firstborn**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [the son born before others]

The phrase **will rise up upon the name of his brother who died** is a common expression of this culture to mean “will carry on the family line of his deceased brother.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be considered the son of his dead uncle] or [will legally represent his dead uncle’s family line]

Here Moses is speaking of a man’s name as if it were an inscription that could be **wiped out**. He means that people would no longer remember that man as part of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his name will not disappear from Israel] or [and his name will not be forgotten in Israel]

The expression **will not be wiped out** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will not let his name disappear]

Here, **name** represents the person’s family line continued through his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his memory] or [his line of descendants]

7.note: Moses assumes that readers will know that city leaders conducted public business at **the gate** of the city. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the place where the elders meet]
See how you translated the similar expression “will rise up upon the name of his brother who died” in the previous verse.

Here, **a name** represents having sons who will continue a family line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a son to continue his family line] or [descendants to carry on his family name]
See how you translated the related expression, “be her brother-in-law” in verse 5.

8.note: By **he stands**, Moses means that the man presents himself formally before the elders to give his testimony. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [If he comes before them to testify] or [If he presents himself before them]

9.q: וְ⁠חָלְצָ֤ה נַעֲל⁠וֹ֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל רַגְל֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠יָרְקָ֖ה בְּ⁠פָנָ֑י⁠ו
9.note: The actions **take off his sandal from his foot and spit in his face** were symbolic actions by which the widow showed that her brother-in-law would not receive any of his brother’s property because he had refused to fulfill his duty and was bringing shame on himself and his brother’s house. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and remove his sandal and spit in his face to show that he had brought disgrace on himself]

Here, **before the eyes** represents sight or witnessing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with the elders as witnesses] or [in the sight of the elders]

Here Moses is speaking of having children and continuing a family line as if it were **building up a house**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [does not continue his brother’s family line] or [does not provide descendants for his brother]

The term **and say** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. Alternate translation: [And she shall respond]

The widow is expected to **respond** with the following statement as part of this legal action against her brother-in-law rather than as an answer to what someone said to her. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And she shall explain her action by saying]

10.note: The expression **be called** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people will call him] or [And people will then say about him]

Here, **name** represents the man’s family line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [his family] or [his line of descendants]

Here Moses is speaking of this man’s family as if it were physically a **house**, and he refers to the man’s disgrace by referring to the **sandal** that his brother’s widow removed from his foot. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The family of the disgraced man] or [The family of the man who refused his duty]

11.note: Here Moses is using the term **brother** to describe fellow Israelites who are not necessarily siblings. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fellow Israelite] or [another man]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the control of his attacker] or [from his attacker’s grasp]

12.note: The expression **your eye shall have no pity** is a common expression of this culture that means “do not show mercy” or “do not feel sorry for her and let her go unpunished.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [show her no mercy] or [punish her without pity]

13.note: Moses is using **a stone and a stone** as a common expression of his culture to refer to two different stones of different weights, **a large and a small**, used for weighing goods. This refers to a **stone** people used as a standard weight. Merchants could deceive and cheat their customers by using stones of different weights that he pretends are the same. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unequal weights]

14.note: Moses is using **an ephah and an ephah** as a common expression of his culture to refer to two different measurements, **a large and a small**, used for measuring amounts of grain. The **ephah** was a standard measure for weighing grain. This is referring to different measurements that someone pretends are the same in order to deceive and cheat someone else. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [unequal measurements]

15.q: אֶ֣בֶן שְׁלֵמָ֤ה וָ⁠צֶ֨דֶק֙ & אֵיפָ֧ה שְׁלֵמָ֛ה וָ⁠צֶ֖דֶק
15.note: The terms **perfect** and **just** expresses a single idea. The word **perfect** tells more about **just**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [A completely accurate weight … a completely accurate measure]
See how you translated the similar phrase “prolong your days” in 4:26. Alternate translation: [you will enjoy many years] or [you will have a long life]

Here, **so that** marks God’s promise of long life as the goal or purpose of having honest weights and measures. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to live many years]
See how you translated the phrase “Yahweh your God” in 1:10.

16.note: The word **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because] or [The reason for this is that]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **injustice** and **abomination**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [these unjust things and act wickedly are detestable]

17.note: Here, **what Amalek did to you** represents what the Amalekite people did to the ancestors of those Moses is addressing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.
The word **you** is plural here, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

18.note: The terms **faint** and **weary** mean similar things. Moses is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [were completely exhausted]

Moses is using **did not fear God** as a common expression of his culture to mean “showed no respect for what God required.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he had no moral principles] or [and he was willing to do terrible things because he did not respect God]

19.note: Here Moses is speaking of security from enemies as if it were physical **rest**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has made you secure] or [has given you peace]

Moses speaks of destroying the Amalekites as if that would **wipe out** the memory of these people like words written on paper. Yahweh means that he will remove the memory of everything about them. See how you translated the very similar phrase “wipe out their name from under the heavens” in 9:14. Alternate translation: [you must destroy the Amalekites so that nobody will remember them anymore]
